label: What is your company's full legal name?
description: This name is printed on every invoice, order and report. Most businesses enter the exact name on their incorporation or GST certificate. A name that does not match your registration causes problems with customers' accounts teams and tax filings.

label: Which country is your company registered in?
description: This loads the right chart of accounts, currency and tax set-up. Most businesses choose the country where they pay tax. A wrong country loads the wrong accounts, which then have to be undone by hand.

label: What is your company's PAN?
description: This is your main tax identity and appears on documents that need it. Indian companies enter their ten-character PAN here. A missing or wrong PAN leads to rejected TDS returns and problems when customers deduct tax from your payments.

label: What is the first line of your registered address?
description: This is printed on your invoices and used for e-way bills. Enter the building, plot or street exactly as on your GST certificate. An address that differs from your registration can make customers' tax credits harder to claim.

label: Which city or town is it in?
description: This completes your printed address. Enter the city as on official papers. Spelling it differently in different places makes reports by location unreliable.

label: Which state is it in?
description: The state decides whether a sale is taxed as local or inter-state GST. Enter the state where you are registered for GST. A wrong state charges the wrong tax on every invoice.

label: What is the PIN code?
description: This is needed for e-way bills and distance calculation. Enter the six-digit PIN code. A wrong code makes e-way bills fail or show the wrong distance.

label: Which day of the week are you closed?
description: This day is marked as a holiday every week for attendance, machine planning and delivery dates. Most Indian businesses choose Sunday. Getting it wrong spoils attendance, payroll and production schedules.
options:
Sunday
Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
Saturday

label: Do you also close on some Saturdays, such as the second and fourth?
description: This decides whether extra weekly holidays need adding to the list. Many factories and offices close on alternate Saturdays. Leaving these out counts those days as absences in attendance and payroll.

label: On what date does your financial year start?
description: This sets where your yearly profit and loss begins; the end date and year name are worked out for you. Almost every Indian business starts on 1 April. A wrong date means your annual figures will not match your tax return.

label: From what date will you start recording transactions in ERPNext?
description: Opening balances for accounts, stock, customers and suppliers are entered as at this date. Most businesses pick the first day of a month or quarter. A date chosen mid-month makes it hard to match your old books with the new ones.

label: Which bank do you mainly use for business?
description: This lets payments and bank statements be matched to the right bank. Most businesses add their main current account first. Without it, payments cannot be reconciled against your statement.

label: What is your bank account number?
description: This is printed on invoices so customers know where to pay. Enter it exactly as on your cheque book. A single wrong digit sends customer payments to the wrong place.

label: What is the IFSC code of your branch?
description: Customers need this to pay you by NEFT or RTGS. It is the eleven-character code on your cheque book. A wrong code makes transfers fail.

label: What do you call your usual credit arrangement with customers?
description: This names the rule used to work out when an invoice is due. Most businesses use a label such as "Net 30". A clear name makes it easy to pick the right terms on each invoice.

label: How many days after the invoice do customers normally pay?
description: This sets due dates and drives your overdue reports. Most Indian businesses give 30 or 45 days. Too long hides late payers; too short makes everyone look overdue.

label: Which payment terms should new customers get by default?
description: These terms are filled in on invoices unless a customer has their own. Most businesses choose their usual credit terms. Left blank, every invoice falls due immediately and overdue reports become meaningless.

label: What is the most a customer may owe you before new orders are stopped?
description: This is the default credit limit for customers who have none of their own; zero means no limit. Many businesses set a figure close to two months of a typical customer's purchases. Too low blocks genuine orders; too high lets bad debts build up.

label: Who may approve an order for a customer who is over their credit limit?
description: People with this role can go past a customer's credit limit; everyone else is stopped. Most businesses give this to the accounts manager only. Leaving it blank means nobody can release a held order, or the limit has to be raised every time.

label: By what percentage may an invoice exceed the order amount?
description: This stops staff invoicing more than was agreed. Most businesses set zero or a small figure for rounding. Too high a figure lets overcharging go unnoticed.

label: Should the system stop the same supplier bill number being entered twice?
description: This guards against paying a supplier twice for one bill. Most businesses say yes. Without it, a duplicate bill can go unnoticed until the supplier has been overpaid.

label: When an invoice is cancelled, should its payment be freed up automatically?
description: If yes, a payment against a cancelled invoice is released so it can be matched to another one. Most businesses say yes. If no, every correction needs the payment unlinked by hand first.

label: Should invoices copy the payment terms from the order automatically?
description: If yes, the due dates agreed on the order carry through to the invoice. Most businesses that agree terms per order say yes. If no, staff must re-enter terms and agreed credit periods get lost.

label: Should advances from customers and to suppliers be kept in their own accounts?
description: If yes, money received or paid before an invoice sits in a separate advance account until it is matched. Businesses that take many advances, and need them shown clearly for GST, usually say yes. If no, advances are mixed into the customer or supplier balance and are harder to track.

label: Do you want to see profit separately for each branch, plant or division?
description: This decides whether to add cost centres beyond the one created for your company. Single-site businesses usually say no. Saying yes without a real need adds an extra field to every transaction.

label: What is the name of a branch or division you want to track separately?
description: Each name becomes a place income and costs can be charged to. Most businesses name them after sites or business lines. Too many make reports hard to read and entries easy to misfile.

label: Is your business registered for GST?
description: This decides whether GST is added to invoices and bills. Almost every Indian business above the turnover threshold says yes. A wrong answer means invoices charge tax you cannot collect or miss tax you owe.

label: Do you deduct TDS when paying suppliers, contractors or professionals?
description: This decides whether tax deduction rules are set up on purchases. Most companies and larger firms say yes. Getting it wrong leads to short deductions, interest and mismatched TDS returns.

label: Is there a group of sales taxed differently, such as exports or SEZ customers?
description: Each answer becomes a tax category so the right tax is picked for those customers automatically. Exporters and SEZ suppliers usually add one; others leave it blank. Without it, staff change taxes by hand and errors follow.

label: Do you buy or sell in any currency other than rupees?
description: This decides whether exchange rates and gain or loss on exchange need setting up. Importers and exporters say yes. Saying no when you do trade abroad leaves exchange differences sitting unexplained in your accounts.

label: Do you keep stock anywhere other than your main store?
description: A store, work-in-progress, finished goods and transit location are already created for you. Say yes only if you have further godowns, shops or sites. Saying no when you have several sites means you cannot see where stock actually is.

label: What is the name of your other stock location?
description: Each location becomes a warehouse so stock can be counted and moved between them. Most businesses name them after the area or building. Names that are too alike lead to stock booked to the wrong place.

label: Where do you keep goods that fail inspection or come back faulty?
description: A separate location keeps rejected goods out of saleable stock. Businesses that inspect incoming material usually create one. Without it, faulty goods count as available and may be sold or used by mistake.

label: Will you give each item your own code, or let the system number them?
description: This decides how new items are identified. Businesses that already have product codes choose Item Code; others let the system number them. Mixing approaches later makes the item list hard to search.

label: How should the cost of stock be worked out?
description: FIFO assumes the oldest stock is used first; Moving Average blends all purchase prices. Most Indian businesses choose FIFO; those with steady prices often prefer Moving Average. It cannot be changed for an item once it has transactions.

label: May staff dispatch goods the system shows as out of stock?
description: If yes, deliveries go ahead even when recorded stock is too low. Most businesses say no to keep stock figures honest. Saying yes hides missing receipts and gives wrong stock values in the accounts.

label: By what percentage may you deliver or receive more than was ordered?
description: This allows small excesses, such as a supplier sending a few extra kilos. Businesses dealing by weight or length often allow 2 to 5 per cent; others keep zero. Too high lets large unordered quantities slip in unchecked.

label: Who may approve receiving or delivering beyond that allowance?
description: People with this role can go past the allowance when there is a genuine reason. Most businesses give it to the store or purchase manager. Without anyone, legitimate excess deliveries cannot be booked at all.

label: Should purchase requests be raised automatically when stock falls below its reorder level?
description: If yes, the system creates material requests for items that fall below the levels you set on them. Businesses with regular consumable or raw material use usually say yes. If no, someone must watch stock levels by hand and shortages are easily missed.

label: Do you need to set stock aside for particular customer orders?
description: If yes, stock can be reserved against a sales order so nobody else can use it. Businesses that hold goods for confirmed orders usually say yes. Without it, reserved goods can be dispatched to another customer by mistake.

label: Do you inspect goods when they arrive or before they leave?
description: This decides whether quality inspection steps are added to receipts and deliveries. Manufacturers and food or pharma businesses usually say yes. Saying no means there is no record of what was checked, which matters for complaints and audits.

label: What do you call the checklist used to inspect your main material?
description: A template holds the list of checks, so inspectors fill in the same points each time. Most businesses name it after the material being checked. Without templates, inspections are inconsistent and hard to compare.

label: If an inspection has not been completed, should the receipt or delivery be stopped or just warned?
description: Stop blocks the transaction until the inspection is finished; Warn lets it through with a message. Businesses where quality is critical choose Stop. Warn on its own is easily ignored, so uninspected goods slip through.

label: What is a main category of products you sell or buy?
description: Groups such as Products, Raw Material, Services and Consumable already exist; add categories that match your range. Most businesses add a handful. Too many make reports cluttered and items hard to file.

label: Do any of your products need to be traced by batch or lot, or have an expiry date?
description: This decides whether batch tracking is switched on for those items. Food, pharma and chemical businesses say yes. It cannot be switched off once an item has stock, so only say yes where you really need it.

label: Do any of your products carry an individual serial number for warranty or service?
description: This decides whether serial number tracking is switched on for those items. Machinery and electronics sellers say yes. Saying yes for low-value goods means a number must be entered for every unit moved.

label: Do you charge different prices to different types of customer?
description: One selling and one buying price list already exist. Say yes if you have, for example, separate wholesale and retail rates. Saying no when you do leads to prices typed by hand and invoice errors.

label: What is the name of your other price list?
description: Each price list holds one set of rates that can be linked to certain customers. Most businesses name it after the customer type. Without it, staff must remember special rates and get some wrong.

label: What type of customer do you have that is not Commercial, Individual, Government or Non Profit?
description: Those four groups already exist; add your own to report sales by customer type. Distributors, dealers and retailers are common additions. Without suitable groups you cannot see which kind of customer is most profitable.

label: Which region or state do you sell into most?
description: Territories let you see sales by area and set targets for salespeople. Most Indian businesses add the states or zones they cover. Leaving everyone in one territory makes regional reports impossible.

label: Who is one of your salespeople?
description: Salespeople are credited on orders so you can track their sales and commission. Businesses with a sales team add each person. Without them you cannot see who brought in which business.

label: What commission percentage does this salesperson earn?
description: This is used to work out commission on their sales. Many businesses pay between 1 and 5 per cent; enter zero if none. A wrong figure leads to overpayment or disputes at month end.

label: Should customers be identified by their name or by a customer code?
description: Customer Name is simplest; Naming Series gives each customer a running code. Businesses with many similarly named customers, or codes already in use, choose Naming Series. Changing approach later leaves a mixed and confusing customer list.
options:
Customer Name
Naming Series
Auto Name

label: Must every sale start with a sales order?
description: If yes, invoices and deliveries can only be made against an order. Make-to-order businesses say yes; counter sales say no. Saying yes when you sell over the counter slows every sale.

label: Must goods be dispatched before they can be invoiced?
description: If yes, every invoice must follow a delivery note. Businesses that dispatch separately from billing say yes. Saying no when you do deliver separately lets stock and invoices drift apart.

label: May sales staff change list prices on an order?
description: If no, staff must use the price list and show any discount separately. Most businesses say no to keep discounts visible. Saying yes lets prices be cut with no record of the discount.

label: Must the invoice price match the order price exactly?
description: If yes, the rate cannot change between quotation, order and invoice. Businesses with agreed contract prices say yes. If no, prices can be altered at invoicing without anyone noticing.

label: May the same item appear more than once on one order?
description: If yes, an item can be listed on several lines, for example with different delivery dates. Businesses with staggered deliveries say yes. If no, such orders must be split or entered awkwardly.

label: May a customer's purchase order number be used on more than one sales order?
description: If yes, one customer PO can be split across several of your sales orders. Businesses supplying large customers against rate contracts often say yes. If no, the system blocks repeat use to stop orders being entered twice.

label: What is a main type of supplier you buy from?
description: Supplier groups let you see spending by type of supplier. Most businesses group by what they buy, such as raw material or services. Without groups, purchase reports are one long list.

label: Should suppliers be identified by their name or by a supplier code?
description: Supplier Name is simplest; Naming Series gives each supplier a running code. Businesses with codes already in use choose Naming Series. Changing approach later leaves a confusing supplier list.
options:
Supplier Name
Naming Series
Auto Name

label: Must every purchase have an approved purchase order?
description: If yes, bills and receipts can only be entered against an order. Businesses wanting control over spending say yes. Saying no lets purchases happen without approval.

label: Must goods be received before the supplier's bill is entered?
description: If yes, you can only book a bill for goods that have arrived. Most stock-holding businesses say yes. Saying no risks paying for goods never received.

label: Must the supplier's bill match the purchase order price exactly?
description: If yes, a bill at a different rate from the order is blocked. Businesses with fixed supplier prices say yes. If no, price increases can be paid without anyone approving them.

label: May the same item appear more than once on one purchase order?
description: If yes, an item can be listed on several lines, for example for staggered deliveries. Businesses ordering in instalments say yes. If no, such orders must be split.

label: Does your supplier still bill you for goods you reject on arrival?
description: If yes, rejected quantities are included in the purchase bill and handled through a return. Most businesses say no, as rejected goods go straight back. A wrong answer means bills that do not match what the supplier actually charged.

label: Do you want to track enquiries before they become customers?
description: This decides whether leads and opportunities are used. Businesses with a sales pipeline say yes; those selling only to existing customers say no. Saying no means follow-ups live in notebooks and lost deals go unnoticed.

label: May the same email address be entered as more than one enquiry?
description: If no, the system warns when someone already recorded enquires again. Most businesses say no so two salespeople do not chase the same person. Saying yes leads to duplicate records and confused follow-ups.

label: For how many days are your quotations normally valid?
description: This fills in the expiry date on new quotations. Most businesses quote for 15 or 30 days, shorter when raw material prices move quickly. Too long commits you to old prices after costs have risen.

label: After how many days without a reply should an open opportunity be closed?
description: Opportunities that have been answered but not followed up are closed after this many days. Many businesses choose 15 to 30 days. Too short closes live deals; too long fills the pipeline with dead ones.

label: Do you make or assemble any of the products you sell?
description: This decides whether bills of materials, work orders and production tracking are set up. Traders and service businesses say no. Saying no when you do manufacture leaves product costs as guesses.

label: Do you send material to other firms to process for you, such as printing or job work?
description: This decides whether subcontracting orders are set up to track material sent out and goods returned. Many Indian manufacturers use job workers for some stages. Without it, material at the job worker disappears from your stock records.

label: Should materials used be taken from the recipe or from what was actually sent to the floor?
description: BOM deducts standard quantities from the recipe; Material Transferred deducts what was actually issued. Businesses with variable wastage choose Material Transferred. The wrong choice makes product costs and stock drift from reality.

label: Do you record material used during production, not just at the end?
description: If yes, consumption can be booked in stages while a job is running. Long-running or process jobs usually say yes. If no, all material is booked only when finished goods are made, so work-in-progress values are wrong in between.

label: By what percentage may planned production exceed what customers have ordered?
description: This allows making a little extra beyond the sales order. Businesses that expect rejections often allow 5 to 10 per cent. Too high ties up material and cash in unsold stock.

label: By what percentage may actual output exceed the work order quantity?
description: This lets the floor book slightly more finished goods than planned. Many businesses allow 0 to 5 per cent. Too high hides overuse of material and makes yields look better than they are.

label: Should batch or serial numbers for finished goods be created from the work order?
description: If yes, numbers are generated as soon as production is planned, so labels can be printed in advance. Businesses that label goods on the line say yes. If no, numbers must be created by hand when goods are finished.

label: Should product cost sheets update automatically when material prices change?
description: If yes, the cost on each bill of materials is refreshed from the latest prices. Businesses with frequently changing raw material prices say yes. If no, quotations may be based on old, too-low costs.

label: Should automatic planning of machine time be switched off?
description: If no, operations are scheduled on workstations according to their working hours so jobs do not clash. Businesses with busy, shared machines answer no; simple workshops often answer yes. Leaving planning on without accurate operation times produces unrealistic schedules.

label: May jobs be scheduled beyond normal working hours?
description: If yes, operations can run past a workstation's working hours. Businesses that run overtime regularly say yes. If no, jobs that do not fit in a shift are pushed to the next day.

label: Do you ever run production on holidays?
description: If yes, jobs may be scheduled on days in the holiday list. Continuous-process plants say yes. If no, planned dates skip holidays even when the plant is actually running.

label: What is one of your main machines or production lines?
description: Workstations are where operations happen and carry the running cost used in product costing. Most businesses add each key machine or line. Leaving them out removes machine and labour cost from product costs.

label: What does an hour on this machine cost you?
description: This hourly figure is added to the cost of every job run here — labour, power and the share of rent the machine takes. Work it out from what the machine and its operators cost in a month, divided by the hours it runs. A wrong figure makes products look more or less profitable than they are.

label: Do you carry out jobs for customers that you bill by time or milestone?
description: This decides whether projects, tasks and timesheets are set up. Contractors, installers and service firms say yes. Saying no when you do run projects means time spent is never billed or costed.

label: Should recorded hours be pulled into the customer's invoice automatically?
description: If yes, a project's timesheets can be added to its invoice in one step. Businesses billing by the hour say yes. If no, hours are copied by hand and some get missed.

label: May one person record time on two jobs at the same moment?
description: If no, the system blocks timesheets that overlap for the same employee. Most businesses say no to keep billing honest. Saying yes allows the same hours to be billed twice.

label: What is a main kind of work you charge customers for?
description: Activity types group time so it can be priced and reported. Most businesses list a few, such as installation or site visit. Without them, all time looks the same and cannot be priced differently.

label: What do you charge the customer per hour for this work?
description: This rate is used when hours are billed. Enter your standard hourly charge in rupees. A wrong rate under- or over-charges every invoice that uses it.

label: What does an hour of this work cost you?
description: This is used to work out the cost and profit of each project. Base it on the wages of the people doing the work. Without it, projects show income but no cost, so every job looks profitable.

label: What department do you have that is not already listed, such as Accounts, Sales, Purchase, Production or HR?
description: The common departments already exist; add any others you use. Manufacturers often add departments for specific production stages. Missing departments file staff under the wrong area in reports.

label: What job title do you use that is not in the standard list?
description: Common titles such as Manager and Accountant already exist; add the ones your staff actually hold. Most businesses add shop-floor and specialist roles. Wrong titles make staff records and letters inaccurate.

label: If staff work at more than one site, what is one site called?
description: Branches group employees by where they work. Single-site businesses leave this blank. Without branches you cannot report headcount or attendance by site.

label: How should employees be identified: by a running number, your own employee number, or their name?
description: This decides the ID shown on payslips, attendance and approvals. Businesses with existing employee codes choose Employee Number. Changing it later leaves a mix of ID styles across records.
options:
Naming Series
Employee Number
Full Name

label: At what age do employees retire?
description: This works out each employee's retirement date from their date of birth. Most Indian private companies use 58 or 60. A wrong age gives wrong retirement dates and gratuity planning.

label: How many hours make a normal working day?
description: This is used to judge full days, half days and overtime. Most factories use 8 or 9 hours. A wrong figure marks people short or gives overtime that was not worked.

label: Must every leave request name the person who will approve it?
description: If yes, leave cannot be applied for without choosing an approver. Most businesses say yes so requests reach the right manager. If no, requests can sit unanswered with nobody responsible.

label: Must every expense claim name the person who will approve it?
description: If yes, claims cannot be submitted without an approver. Most businesses say yes to control reimbursements. If no, claims may be paid without anyone checking them.

label: Should salary be worked out from leave taken or from daily attendance?
description: Leave assumes full attendance unless leave is recorded; Attendance pays only for days marked present. Factories with biometric attendance usually choose Attendance; offices often choose Leave. The wrong choice pays people for days they did not work, or docks days they did.

label: Should holidays count as working days when working out a day's pay?
description: If yes, monthly salary is divided by all days in the month; if no, by working days only. Most Indian businesses pay on calendar days and say yes. The choice changes the deduction for each absent day.

label: If no attendance is recorded for a day, should the person be treated as present or absent?
description: This decides how gaps in attendance affect pay. Businesses with reliable biometric records choose Absent; others choose Present. Choosing Absent with patchy records cuts pay unfairly.

label: Do you want to track machinery, vehicles or equipment and their depreciation?
description: This decides whether asset records and automatic depreciation are set up. Manufacturers and businesses with vehicles say yes. Saying no means depreciation is worked out and entered by hand each year.

label: What is a main type of asset you own?
description: Categories hold the depreciation rules shared by similar assets. Most businesses follow the blocks in their depreciation schedule, such as plant and machinery or vehicles. Grouping unlike assets together gives them the wrong depreciation.

label: Do assets in this category take time to build or install before use?
description: If yes, costs are held as capital work in progress until the asset is ready, and depreciation starts only then. Businesses installing plant or building sheds say yes. If no, depreciation may start before the asset is actually in use.

label: How should assets in this category lose value?
description: Straight Line spreads cost evenly; Written Down Value takes a fixed percentage of what remains. Many Indian companies use Written Down Value. The wrong method puts your asset values out of line with your auditor's figures.
options:
Straight Line
Double Declining Balance
Written Down Value
Manual

label: Over how many periods should these assets be depreciated?
description: This is the useful life counted in depreciation periods. With yearly depreciation, plant and machinery is commonly spread over about 15 periods. Too few or too many misstates asset values and yearly profit.

label: How many months apart should depreciation be booked?
description: This sets how often depreciation entries are posted. Choose 12 for yearly or 1 for monthly accounts. Monthly gives truer monthly profit but creates many more entries.

label: Should depreciation be posted to the accounts automatically when due?
description: If yes, scheduled depreciation entries are booked on their dates without anyone acting. Most businesses say yes. If no, someone must post them by hand and missed entries overstate profit.

label: Where are most of your assets kept?
description: Each asset must be linked to a location so it can be found and verified. Most businesses add each site or building. Without locations, physical checks of assets become guesswork.
